value.overview: The Black-capped Flycatcher is a small, distinctive tyrant flycatcher of the high mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is especially associated with cool, humid upland forests and forest edges, where it watches from exposed perches and makes short flights to catch insects. Its black crown and strong pale eye-ring make it more recognizable than many similar Empidonax flycatchers. Costa Rica contains most of the species’ range and is an important center for its population.
value.classification: The Black-capped Flycatcher belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Empidonax. It is generally treated as a monotypic species, without currently recognized subspecies.
value.identification: This very small flycatcher has a dark blackish crown, sometimes forming a short crest, and a conspicuous white eye-ring that is often broader behind the eye. The upperparts are brownish olive, with dusky wings, pale-edged feathers, and two subtle wing-bars. The throat is whitish or grayish buff, while the breast and belly are pale buff to cinnamon. The bill has a dark upper mandible and an orange-yellow lower mandible with a dark tip. Juveniles are duller and browner.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs in Costa Rica and western Panama, mainly in highland regions. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the Central Volcanic Cordillera, the Dota area, and the Cordillera de Talamanca, including high-elevation sites such as the Irazú, Turrialba, and Talamanca mountain regions. It usually occupies humid montane evergreen forest, high-elevation oak woodland, forest edges, shrubby second growth, and wooded pastures. It is most often found around 2,100–3,300 meters, sometimes descending lower during the rainy season.
value.migrationStatus: It is essentially resident in Costa Rica and does not undertake long-distance migration. Individuals may make local or seasonal movements to lower elevations, especially during the rainy season, with records possible around 1,850–2,100 meters.
value.breeding: Breeding has been recorded mainly from March through May. The nest is an open cup made from grass and moss and lined with fine plant fibers and other soft materials. It may be placed in a fork of a tree or shrub several meters above the ground, or attached to drooping grass over an earthen bank. The usual clutch is two pale, unmarked eggs. Details of incubation, nestling development, and parental care remain poorly documented.
value.dietFeeding: The Black-capped Flycatcher feeds mainly on flying insects and other small arthropods. It commonly hunts from a high perch in the forest canopy, but uses bushes, fence posts, and other exposed perches in open habitat. From the perch it makes short aerial sallies to capture prey, often returning to the same spot. It may briefly quiver its tail after landing. Foraging can occur alone or near other insect-eating birds.
value.behavior: This flycatcher is generally active and alert, often sitting upright on an exposed branch while scanning for prey. It frequently repeats short flights from a regular perch and may defend a breeding territory with sharp calls and chases. Vocalizations include emphatic notes during the breeding season and simpler chips or whistles at other times. Outside the breeding period, it is often solitary, although it may forage near mixed-species groups in suitable montane habitat.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable, although precise population estimates and long-term monitoring data are limited.
